extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of journalism, political science, public opinion, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying principles about how public opinion is formed, distorted, and communicated (role of language, stereotypes, attention, environment, and media). Useful for evaluating media, propaganda, or civic discourse quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words as tokens of value / word-currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are tokens of value that represent meaning whose 'representative value' fluctuates across time, cultures, and circumstances (a 'word-currency' subject to inflation or war fluctuations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting foreign or historical language, mentally 'translate' by adjusting for cultural and temporal exchange rates (examples: Bossuet's 'etonnant' vs modern French usage; English 'awful'). Beware that comparable praises or labels ('a distinguished scholar', 'a clever writer') map differently between languages. Note the author's banking metaphor: in normal times exchange might be 25, in war 46 — apply a similar mental exchange when reading foreign press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion is largely constructed in imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the world is vast and direct experience limited, most opinions are pieced together from reports and imagination rather than direct observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that single words (e.g., 'Mexico', 'Japan') evoke composite, often stereotyped images rather than accurate, detailed knowledge. When evaluating public opinion, account for the constructed, composite nature of the mental images behind labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels evoke culturally-shaped composite images
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain country or group names immediately evoke a culturally-influenced composite of images (e.g., 'Mexico' as sand, cactus, greasers; 'Japan' as slant-eyed stereotypes, samurai, cherry blossoms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor and question the stereotyped composites evoked by labels; seek more precise, varied information rather than relying on quick associative images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise legal/technical terms over vague political phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words (e.g., 'alien') are unusually exact legal terms, while terms like 'sovereignty', 'independence', 'national honor', 'imperialism', 'capitalism', 'socialism' are much vaguer and invite partisan stances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When clarity is required, use or seek precise definitions; be cautious of taking sides based on vague political vocabulary which conceals differing senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity of mind = ability to dissociate analogies and attend to differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Lucidity (the power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety) is a relative cognitive faculty varying greatly across individuals and groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of public judgement should account for varying levels of lucidity; expect coarser discrimination in some populations and finer discrimination among experts or those with direct involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise and personal engagement sharpen perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership, practice, or passionate involvement (hobby/expertise) projects attention and yields much finer discrimination (e.g., an owner noticing carburetor differences that a casual rider would not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for domain expertise when evaluating reported perceptions: direct involvement tends to produce three-dimensional, detailed understanding compared with superficial or generalized views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fatigue and distraction flatten discrimination (laboratory evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological experiments (association tests) show that slight mental fatigue, inner disturbance, or external distraction 'flatten' the quality of response, increasing primitive associations (clang responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of opinions formed under fatigue/distraction (e.g., commuters reading newspapers in noisy streetcars); expect less accurate political judgments when attention conditions are poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban/industrial environment degrades attention and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: City life — noise, odor, heat, crowds, incessant distractions — reduces solitude and silence, undermining the intellectual conditions needed for clear discriminations and good political judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret mass urban opinion with caution: design of work/life (long hours, monotony, poor housing) contributes to 'automatism' and flickering attention that favors sensational headlines and catch-words over careful thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving physical conditions helps but is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Movements for shorter workdays, longer vacations, better light/air/order address necessary material preconditions for thought but are only the beginning for improving intellectual quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or media reforms should complement physical improvements with efforts to nurture more sustained, three-dimensional engagement and inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional conflicts and unconscious complexes distort association
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional conflicts (ambition, economic interest, personal animosity, racial prejudice, class feeling) can dramatically alter speed, accuracy, and quality of association, causing variable or failed responses to stimuli.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variability and distortion in public responses where 'hot' emotional themes are involved; factor in affective drivers when analyzing opinion or survey responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass composition lowers average attention: account for low-capacity audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Because large segments of the public include illiterate, feeble-minded, neurotic, undernourished, or frustrated individuals, popular appeals must reckon with audiences whose lives supply little relevant experience for the issues discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messaging and evaluation with awareness that broad popular streams will encounter cognitive limitations, producing misunderstandings and prejudiced analogies; targeted education and communication strategies are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad vs narrow appeals — psychic level determines audience size
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'broad appeal' addresses susceptibilities widely distributed; a 'narrow' or 'special' appeal targets uncommon susceptibilities. The psychic level where a stimulus acts determines the potential audience size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or judging persuasion, identify whether the appeal relies on common, shallow susceptibilities (faces, simple symbols) or specialized, rare distinctions; the same person may respond differently at different levels depending on context (e.g., starving vs culturally cultivated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental filtering of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to facts is refracted by censorship and privacy at the source, physical and social barriers at reception, scanty attention, poverty of language, distraction, unconscious constellations of feeling, and wear and tear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate information flow by tracing these filters; recognize that multiple limitations combine to produce obscurity, misleading fictions, lack of checks on deliberate misleaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes: we define first, then see
rubrics_metrics.description: People typically apply pre-existing definitions and stereotypes first and then perceive the world through those lenses; stereotypes preempt and reshape incoming information (e.g., eyewitnesses recalling scenes shaped by stereotyped images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat eyewitness reports and visual descriptions as partly constructed; training and critical methods reduce but do not eliminate stereotype-driven errors. Use multiple independent observations and context appraisal to mitigate stereotype effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of stereotypes: art, social codes, media (cinema) and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotyped shapes are lent to our perception not only by art but by moral codes, social philosophies, political agitations, and especially by mass media like cinema which standardize imagery across the populace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how cultural products and media cultivate shared images that then structure public perception; be alert to the dominance of mass visual media in forming mental pictures invoked by words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and risk of stereotypes — hold them lightly and investigate origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes economize attention and are often necessary, but their character and the gullibility with which we use them determine whether they help or mislead; education and historical awareness can reveal the origins of preconceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to discard all stereotypes (impractical), but scrutinize their provenance, modify them when warranted, and cultivate a philosophy of life that recognizes their provisional nature; useful history is 'antiseptic' in showing how ideas were planted.

rubrics_metrics.name: To judge actors, appraise their available information and filtering minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding other people's actions requires appraising not only the information they had but also the minds through which that information was filtered (their stereotypes, training, and contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning responsibility or evaluating decisions, consider the cognitive and informational context of actors — what types, standards, or stereotypes shaped their perceptions — rather than judging solely by outcomes.
